tagline: Brick highway remnants trace an earlier journey through Espanola and Bunnell.
intro: Heritage Crossroads is a 98-mile road network centered on Bunnell in northeastern Florida, reaching into Flagler, Volusia and St. Johns counties. Its roads connect the Old Brick Road at Espanola, Bunnell’s US 1 corridor and the eastward drive on State Road 100 to Flagler Beach. Designated on November 19, 2008, the scenic highway is presented by Florida’s Department of Transportation as a route through the region’s settlement and travel history. Near Codys Corner, much of the surrounding land is dedicated to preserves.

The Dixie Highway began as an auto-trail proposal in 1914, promoted by Carl G. Fisher to connect the Midwest and South. It developed into a network of connected roads. At Espanola, highway traffic brought tourists and businesses. Then a new road, now US 1, bypassed the town in 1926, and automobile traffic fell sharply. The Old Brick Road survives as part of the original brick Dixie Highway.

Start at Espanola’s Old Brick Road junction, then head toward Bunnell, the network’s hub. State Road 100 runs eight miles east from Bunnell to Flagler Beach. Bulow Plantation’s ruins lie on a separate excursion south of SR 100. Finish inland at Codys Corner, where Dupont Road meets State Road 11 southwest of Bunnell.

moments.title: Espanola
moments.text: Espanola sits at the junction of Old Brick Road, County Road 13 and County Road 205. The brick road is a surviving section of the original Dixie Highway. The Old Brick Road was completed around 1917. Automobile travelers once supported a hotel and camps here. In 1926, the new highway from St. Augustine directly to Bunnell bypassed Espanola, diverting traffic and damaging the local economy. The old road entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2005. The Florida Department of Transportation identifies the Old Brick Road as a place to walk, cycle or drive.
moments.notice: The Old Brick Road preserves part of the original brick Dixie Highway.

moments.title: Bulow Plantation Ruins Historic State Park
moments.text: The ruined sugar mill is built of coquina, a sedimentary rock made of shells. Enslaved Africans and African Americans supplied the plantation’s forced labor. Charles Wilhelm Bulow began developing the plantation in 1821, making his enslaved workforce clear land for indigo, cotton, rice and sugarcane. His son John Joachim inherited the plantation in 1823 and managed it. The plantation was destroyed in the Seminole War of 1836. Florida acquired the property and ruins in 1945 and dedicated the historic park in 1957. The interpretive center holds original artifacts and exhibits on the plantation.
moments.notice: Shells form the coquina stone used in the ruined sugar mill.

moments.title: Codys Corner
moments.text: At Dupont Road and State Road 11, Codys Corner takes its name from local farmer Richard Cody, Sr., who named it in 1907. It was also called Codyville, the name used in the 1932 US Geological Survey. By the 1950s, it was known for irrigation wells. The Florida Geological Survey reported that artesian wells here, in St. Johns Park and in Bunnell supplied most of the groundwater pumped in the county. Preserve land now occupies much of the surrounding area, including the Relay Tract Conservation Easements just east of the crossroads.
